- Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has reached 3,676 deaths, with 7,614 confirmed cases and a case fatality rate of 48.3% as of mid-September 2026, per the DRC Ministry of Communications and Media. The outbreak remains ongoing in a region afflicted by armed conflict for 30 years, with the UN on August 21 calling for additional resources to control transmission amid massive humanitarian needs. A Nature Medicine study previously indicated the outbreak is caused by a previously unknown Bundibugyo virus strain, likely spillover from animals to humans. The World Health Organization had declared on May 17 that the DRC and Uganda outbreaks constitute a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, with high regional risk.

This effort emphasizes protection of health workers amid ongoing transmission, while the absence of a vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain highlights remaining gaps in outbreak containment.

Outside hosts, viruses are inert; upon entry to humans or animals, they hijack cells and replicate rapidly. Emergence is driven by ecological disruption: deforestation, climate-change–driven heatwaves and heavy rains, increasing contact among people, wildlife, and livestock. Mosquitoes and ticks proliferate, elevating chikungunya risks in metropolitan France and Lyme borreliosis; rodents thrive in warm, damp conditions and can harbor hantaviruses. Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo are linked to bat reservoirs via artisanal mining; fruit contamination can transmit filoviruses. Avian influenza moves from wild birds to poultry and then humans, with US observations of transmission through pigs or cattle in contact with birds. Reservoir hosts may be asymptomatic; viruses often persist stealthily to spread, as with SARS-CoV-2. Emphasis on wildlife surveillance to prevent future epidemics; air travel accelerates spread, not emergence.

triage.headline_ja: 次に出現するウイルスは既に未知の動物リザーバーの中に存在する：将来の流行を防ぐためのウイルス学者の助言

article.articleHeadline: DRC - Cholera in South Kivu: fewer cases than in 2025, and already 61 more deaths.
article.articleSummary: Cholera in South Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, reached 11,854 cases and 160 deaths as of 19 September 2026, with a year-to-date case-fatality around 1.35% (about 1.4%). This year’s deaths are ~62% higher than 99 in 2025, while cases are ~9% lower than 2025’s 13,027. The outbreak is not spreading geographically but is more deadly, reflecting delayed care. Weeks 36–37 saw 7 deaths per 482 cases, then 13 deaths per 651 cases. Bukavu, Kabare, Walungu, and Uvira are hardest hit; in Bukavu’s Ibanda health zone, 167 cases were reported in a single week. By June, 33 of 80 deaths occurred in health facilities, with 47 in the community, signaling gaps in access and response. Ongoing displacement (over 500,000 internally displaced, 110,000+ refugees) and attacks on health facilities, plus chronic water access problems in Ibanda, worsen transmission.

triage.headline_ja: DRC - 南キブ州のコレラ：2026年は症例数は2025年より少ないが、すでに61人多い死者数
triage.triage_reason: 南キブ州で継続中のコレラアウトブレイクにおいて、症例数は減少しているものの死亡数・致死率が前年より大幅に増加しており、避難民・医療アクセス制限などの脆弱性要因も重なっているため、フルリスク評価が必要と判断される。
triage.notes: 既存の継続アウトブレイクだが、致死率が前年比62%増加しており重症化・対応の遅れが懸念される。50万人超の国内避難民、11万人超の難民、医療施設への攻撃、水アクセス問題など複合的な脆弱性要因があり、外部支援の必要性が高いと推察される。

article.articleHeadline: Ebola: One of Africa's Most Feared Diseases, and the Lessons the Continent Is Still Learning
article.articleSummary: DR Congo's Ituri Province confronts Bundibugyo ebolavirus in a high-mortality outbreak. On May 15, 2026, after an alert on May 5, the country declared its 17th Ebola outbreak. Bundibugyo has no licensed vaccine or targeted treatments; past outbreaks show case-fatality 30–50%. As of August 1, 2026, 3,748 confirmed cases and 1,657 deaths reported. Africa CDC and WHO launched a US$518 million joint response plan for June–November. The Lancet notes Africa faces this threat without validated diagnostics or vaccines, while Kinshasa's INRB rapidly confirmed the diagnosis. The PARTNERS trial in DRC tests MBP134 with remdesivir, alone or combined; Uganda's UVRI discusses two candidate Bundibugyo vaccines in early trials. Lomé hosted a September conference urging stronger detection, diagnostic capacity, cross-border coordination, and investment in Africa-led research and manufacturing.

triage.headline_ja: エボラ出血熱：アフリカで最も恐れられる疾病の一つ、そして大陸がいまなお学び続けている教訓
triage.triage_reason: DRCイツリ州で第17次エボラ流行（Bundibugyoエボラウイルス）が進行中で、致死率30-50%、確定例3,748人・死亡1,657人という大規模な公衆衛生危機であり、Africa CDC/WHOが5.18億ドル規模の国際対応計画を発動している。IHR基準・WPRO基準ともに複数該当し社会的関心も高い。
triage.notes: 記事の主題はDRCイツリ州における第17次エボラ流行。ウガンダ・トーゴは会議開催地やワクチン研究協力先として言及されているが、発生国ではないため対象国リストから除外（両国とも対象国リストに含まれていない）。既に大規模流行であり国際対応（Africa CDC/WHO共同計画）が進行中のため、WHO通知済み事案としてPICKUP判定とした。

article.articleHeadline: The Central African President launches a cholera vaccination campaign and administers a dose to the first patient.
article.articleSummary: Cholera vaccination campaign in the Central African Republic targets 611,000 people, with President Faustin Archange Touadéra administering the first oral dose to a patient in Bimbo. The initiative follows a cholera outbreak officially declared on 26 June, with the last confirmed case on 17 July. Measures to curb transmission include water purification products distributed to 3,000 households; more than 600 handwashing devices placed at households along the Ubangi River; nearly 500 households trained in home water purification, hygiene, and waste disposal; disinfection operations and distribution of response kits to affected households. Five mobile laboratories are operational, with five more ready for deployment. Cross-border cooperation has been reinforced with the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of the Congo, Uganda, and South Sudan, as the campaign aims to control transmission across affected regions.

article.articleHeadline: Infectious Information 9/20/2026
article.articleSummary: CDC changes how it records and reports measles and other infectious deaths, prompting criticism from an epidemiologist who says transparency is lacking. Sept 20, 2026: Pennsylvania reports four measles deaths (third on Sept 14, fourth on Sept 15). Johns Hopkins tracker map is cited. Measles is not the only airborne threat: Acinetobacter can spread through the air; all avian-flu varieties remain active in humans, with greater activity in birds. Seasonal influenza spreads easily, and isolation is uncommon. Ebola remains a fluids-transmission risk and is still problematic in the DRC, even as schools reopen with safety measures. MRSA skin infections linked to bouncy castles; several hand soaps recalled. Food outbreaks persist: broccoli and alfalfa sprouts; cross-contamination with radish sprout mixes; lettuce outbreaks; prepared salads, cream cheese; rice with foreign materials. Denmark reports no congenital syphilis in 10 years; probiotics may prevent serious GI complications in premature infants.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in the DRC: "The community must participate as an equal partner".
article.articleSummary: As of 20 September 2026, Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has caused more than 3,500 deaths across seven provinces and over 62 health zones. The outbreak is receding in areas where capacities have been reinforced but is advancing in others, with community deaths persisting. In an interview, Dr. Marie Roseline Belizaire, WHO Africa emergencies director, explains these deaths reflect not only hesitancy but also late alerts, unavailable ambulances, distant centers, or the inability to leave work. "There is not only Ebola that kills in the community"— hunger, malnutrition, insecurity, and lack of clean water fuel the crisis. The response must be locally adapted and proactive, beginning with listening and involving communities at decision tables. Communities must participate as equal partners. She also refutes misinformation and discusses sustaining durable improvements.

article.articleHeadline: "God help us": Gravediggers work nonstop as Ebola kills thousands.
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo persists, with gravediggers working nonstop as the virulent virus claims thousands of lives. Sky News reports that nearly four thousand people have died since May, as frontline healthcare teams operate in conflict zones, confront local skepticism, and face global indifference. Burial crews are compelled to work day and night to entomb victims and curb transmission. Sky's correspondent Stuart Ramsay traversed the red zone to witness how the virus continues to spread and the harsh conditions under which medical staff and communities cope. The coverage highlights the ongoing outbreak, access challenges, and the strain on health systems and public health measures amid conflict.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Kongo: Vaccines Alone Are Not Enough, Says an Expert.
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreaks intensify in the Kongo-Kinshasa region of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with experts warning it could become the largest to date. Virologist and zoonoses specialist Fabian Leendertz (Head, Helmholtz Institute for One Health) notes the epidemic remains out of control, though WHO reports around 85% of contacts are being traced this week—a positive step but not decisive. Vaccines are a key tool, but success depends on public trust; skepticism and misinformation hinder uptake. Local engagement—using community figures such as religious leaders, athletes, and long-standing aid workers—is essential to reach people and improve access. The complex security situation and governance challenges limit aid work, preventing rapid mass vaccination. The 2014–2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, which killed over 11,000, showed that extensive contact tracing, isolation, and changes in burial practices were critical to ending transmission, alongside community cooperation.

article.articleHeadline: Meet Rajarshi Mandal, the 16-year-old Lexington student whose malaria model showed the same mosquito-net supply could prevent twice as many infections; he won $50,000
article.articleSummary: Rajarshi Mandal, a 16-year-old Lexington High School student from Lexington, Massachusetts, built an ordinary differential equation malaria transmission model to optimize the allocation of insecticide-treated bed nets under limited supply. Using a framework that simulates transmission with seasonality, insecticide resistance, net degradation, and remote-area logistics, his results show the same global net supply could prevent twice as many infections if nets are distributed where they have the greatest impact, rather than by population alone. The study addresses backward bifurcation to ensure transmission persistence under realistic conditions and derives a reproduction number reflecting transmission risk. Mandal abandoned an initial Deep Q Network after instability and now directly scores allocations. The work highlights global nets distributed around 200 million annually and earned him a $50,000 Davidson Fellows Scholarship, with an image from the Democratic Republic of Congo illustrating logistical hurdles that can impede even well-planned programs.

article.articleHeadline: Warning: Complications of Influenza A
article.articleSummary: In Hanoi, a 4-year-old girl developed acute necrotizing encephalopathy (ANE) associated with Influenza A after fever and respiratory symptoms. She had continuous seizures and coma within 2 days; a throat swab tested positive for Influenza A. She received high-dose immunosuppressive therapy, renal replacement therapy, and intensive neurocritical care at National Children's Hospital, but brain injury progressed and she died two days after admission. ANE is a rare post-viral brain disease, often following Influenza A, caused by an excessive inflammatory response with cytokine release that disrupts the blood-brain barrier, leading to edema, necrosis, coagulopathy and multi-organ involvement. It typically affects children 2-5 years old. No unified treatment protocol exists; early immunosuppression within 24 hours of neurological symptoms may help some cases. Influenza in children is usually mild but can cause pneumonia, myocarditis, encephalitis, respiratory failure or multi-organ injury. Parents should seek urgent care for high fever with seizures or breathing problems; vaccination is advised.

triage.triage_reason: ハノイで4歳女児がA型インフルエンザに伴う急性壊死性脳症（ANE）で死亡した単一症例報告であり、既知のまれな合併症の枠内にとどまる。集団発生やクラスターを示す情報はなく、フルRRAに進むには情報不足のため経過観察とする。

article.articleHeadline: African swine fever resurges in Nghe An.
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-09-20, African swine fever resurges in Nghệ An Province, Vietnam, with 30 outbreaks reported this year. Over 7,300 pigs have been culled, weighing 442,680 kg, imposing losses mainly on smallholder farmers in mountainous communes. Hotspots include Châu Tiến, Quỳ Châu, Nga My, Tương Dương, Nghĩa Đồng, and Lượng Minh. Officials warn that seasonal transition and flood events heighten transmission risk and complicate control, given dispersed, small-scale farming and some free-ranging practices. After losses, many households rapidly restock while the virus persists in the surrounding environment. The report calls for intensified prevention and surveillance to curb further spread as weather conditions worsen.

article.articleHeadline: Joining forces to combat dengue fever
article.articleSummary: Dong Nai province, Vietnam, faces a dengue fever outbreak with more than 11,500 cases and six deaths reported by August 2026. Bình Phước General Hospital, in the northern part of the province, treated 1,049 dengue patients in eight months of 2026, up 188% from 2025; July and August increases reached 206.7% and 224.9%. The hospital has intensified admission capacity, drugs, and staff training, and reports no severe cases or deaths yet, while coordinating with lower-level facilities. Transmission now extends into urban wards: Nha Bich commune had 111 cases and 58 outbreaks across all seven hamlets by end-August 2026. Bình Phước ward recorded a dengue death in early August 2026. Hung Phuoc commune, a border area with forest reserves and a high ethnic minority population, remains high risk with ongoing community campaigns. Authorities stress environmental sanitation, larval control and eliminating standing water; health departments require real-time reporting and hospital readiness.

article.articleHeadline: A woman with influenza A and pneumonia.
article.articleSummary: Ms. Tinh, a 67-year-old woman in Ho Chi Minh City, was diagnosed with influenza A complicated by pneumonia and bronchospasm. Chest radiography at Tam Anh General Hospital showed diffuse patchy infiltrates in both lungs with left basilar atelectasis. She had myalgia, fever, nasal congestion, and cough, and tested positive for influenza A. Past medical history included dyslipidemia and type 2 diabetes. She received bronchodilators, antivirals, antibiotics, with glycemic and lipid control and inhaled therapy. After 5 days, respiratory status improved, she became afebrile, and cough eased before discharge. Influenza can progress to pneumonia, especially in older adults with chronic diseases; warning signs include dyspnea, tachypnea, chest pain, and fever. Recommendations: annual influenza vaccination, infection control, respiratory hygiene, and early medical evaluation for abnormal signs.

article.articleHeadline: Be wary as Influenza A surges, UGM nutrition expert reveals that the key to immune system strength is not just from medicine.
article.articleSummary: Influenza A cases are rising across age groups in Indonesia, prompting focus beyond medicines to daily nutrition. Dr. Toto Sudargo, a nutrition expert from UNIMUS and UGM, says immunity is built indirectly through a balanced intake of carbohydrates, protein, fats, vitamins, and vegetables. Indonesian eating habits skew toward quick, carb- and fat-heavy meals, with low vegetable consumption, undermining immune defenses rich in vitamin C and antioxidants. For influenza season, emphasis should be on real, balanced food rather than supplements. Key nutrients include protein for immune cell formation, vitamin C and antioxidants from vegetables and fruit, and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K that require fat for absorption. Pro-vitamin A sources such as cassava leaves and Melinjo leaves can be prepared in dishes like sayur lodeh with coconut milk to aid absorption.

article.articleHeadline: Influenza positivity rate rises to 46 percent, Rumkitalmar Ewa Pangalila holds free medical screenings in Surabaya.
article.articleSummary: Influenza positivity nationwide rose to 46% for 13–19 September 2026, up from 35% the prior week, though overall influenza activity remains low. In Surabaya, Rumkitalmar Ewa Pangalila (Navy Hospital) at Lanmar Surabaya opened free screening and treatment on 20 September 2026 for about 2,000 participants, including Marine Corps personnel and the public. The effort follows a Surabaya Health Office circular on early influenza preparedness and includes on-site checks (blood pressure, glucose, cholesterol); those with influenza-like symptoms for Influenza A receive further medical assessment. The initiative also includes blood donation targeting 1,000 donors with UTD RSUD dr. Soetomo Surabaya and 1,000 food packages for attendees. The event coincides with the 81st anniversary of the Indonesian National Armed Forces (TNI), with a related Basic Life Support training nationwide on 19 September 2026 for 81,000 participants.

article.articleHeadline: 12 Under-Five Children Test Positive for Measles, Banjar City Health Office Pursues Immunization for 14,385 Children
article.articleSummary: As of 20 September 2026, Banjar City, West Java, Indonesia, is conducting Outbreak Response Immunization (ORI) after 12 under-five children tested positive for measles by the West Java Provincial Health Laboratory (Labkesda). From January to September 2026, 75 suspected measles cases were reported, with 12 laboratory-confirmed; all recovered following treatment in dedicated wards. To curb transmission, the Health Office mobilized 10 puskesmas to implement ORI targeting 14,385 children. About 2,600 children have already received catch-up immunization through parental education. The free measles vaccination program covers children aged 9 months, 18 months, and first-grade students, regardless of prior immunization status. Health workers are advised to use PPE and masks, maintain distancing, and reinforce hygiene practices. Parents are urged to bring their children for vaccination to build immunity and prevent future outbreaks.

The trial aims to assess whether indoor insecticide-treated paper can significantly reduce indoor mosquito populations and contribute to malaria elimination, though no numerical results are provided yet.

Poultry sheds should avoid extreme temperatures; in heat ensure good ventilation to reduce heat stress, while in cold weather use curtains or tarpaulins to limit cold air. Dr. S. D. Preparedness before seasonal changes reduces risks and losses.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue scare: this time the 'vaccine shield'! India's huge discovery 'Q-Dengue', when will you get it?
article.articleSummary: QDENGA, India's first licensed dengue vaccine, developed jointly by Takeda of Japan and Dr. Reddy's Laboratories, received regulatory approval in 2026 and is expected in Indian markets by early 2027. Based on an attenuated DENV-2 backbone, it elicits immunity against all four dengue serotypes (DENV-1–DENV-4). International trial data show a substantial drop in dengue risk and an 88% reduction in hospitalization among vaccine recipients. Eligibility covers 4–60-year-olds without prior dengue testing; two 0.5 mL doses given at scheduled intervals. Side effects are mild, mainly injection-site pain or low-grade fever. In a country of about 130 crore people, this vaccine could be a game changer for dengue control during monsoon season, complementing vector control and public health measures.

article.articleHeadline: A Dangerous Gastrointestinal Infection Has Adapted to Treatment: Doctors Warn of New Threats to Health.
article.articleSummary: Shigellosis in Kerala, India, shows increasing resistance of Shigella to ampicillin and chloramphenicol, undermining traditional first-line therapy, according to Kerala’s Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network. Shigellosis is an acute diarrheal disease with blood and mucus (dysentery), high fever, and abdominal cramps; youngest children under five are most at risk of dehydration and fatal outcomes. Transmission is fecal-oral through contaminated water, food, hands, and objects, with outbreaks common in areas lacking clean water and sanitation. In recent months, the share of resistant Shigella strains has risen, complicating treatment. Contributing factors include rural delays in seeking care, poor sanitation, and limited access to safe water. Authorities are updating diagnostic and treatment protocols and conducting hygiene campaigns. Experts warn that rising resistance could increase severe complications and limit therapy options, requiring a coordinated health-system response, especially where infrastructure is developing.

Early diagnosis, treatment, and vaccination can safeguard livestock and reduce losses during the rainy season.

article.articleHeadline: Targeted SAP Domain Mutations Weaken Foot-and-Mouth Disease Virus Virulence
article.articleSummary: Foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) Lpro SAP-domain mutations attenuate virulence without compromising replication in cell culture. Indian researchers at ICAR-Indian Veterinary Research Institute (Bengaluru) engineered targeted substitutions in the SAP domain of Lpro within the infectious cDNA clone Asia1/IND/63/1972 (pAsia-WT). Two mutants, pAsia-SAP1 and pAsia-SAP2, were rescued; both showed growth kinetics and plaque morphology indistinguishable from WT in vitro. Serial passage revealed pAsia-SAP2 retained its mutations through twenty passages, whereas pAsia-SAP1 partially reverted at position 55 (S55 reverts; G56 remains). Innate immune gene transcripts were upregulated in SAP1-infected cells but not SAP2-infected cells, indicating differing immune-activation profiles. In suckling mice, SAP2 exhibited markedly reduced pathogenicity with greater survival. These findings suggest SAP-domain mutations as a rational route to attenuated FMDV vaccine strains and illuminate how Lpro coordinates immune evasion, with potential implications for vaccine design and control of outbreaks in veterinary medicine.

article.articleHeadline: Toxoplasma Parasite Found in Nigerian Free-Range Birds, Raising Food Safety
article.articleSummary: Toxoplasma gondii, an intracellular parasite that infects roughly one-third of humans, was detected by DNA in 22 of 162 free-range birds from Nigeria’s Federal Capital Territory, a 13.6% overall rate (95% CI 9.1–19.7%). Chickens yielded 16.7% positives, pigeons 10%, and guinea fowl 6.7%; positives occurred across six area councils. Sampling spanned Aug 2025–Feb 2026 (rainy and dry seasons). Rainy-season prevalence reached 24.7% versus 2.5% in the dry season (odds ratio 12.78). Infected chickens weighed less (mean 1,284.8 g) than negatives (1,819.4 g). Histology of brain/liver in 66 birds revealed no tissue cysts or tachyzoites. Three high-quality B1 gene sequences from chickens showed 100% identity and clustered with reference sequences from Egypt, Iran, Mexico, and India, differing by 2–4 nucleotides from Nigerian Plateau sequences. First molecular evidence of natural infection in African guinea fowl; underscores implications for food safety and zoonotic surveillance in Nigeria.

article.articleHeadline: Lingering Dengue NS1 Antigen Complicates Diagnosis of Visceral
article.articleSummary: 23-year-old migrant worker from Dang district, Nepal, who had worked in Malaysia, presented with prolonged fever after an initial positive dengue NS1 test in Malaysia. Dengue fever persisted, but dengue NS1 antigenemia continued as he returned to Nepal. In India, clinicians evaluated for hematologic malignancy given fever, splenomegaly/hepatomegaly and pancytopenia, delaying VL diagnosis. Visceral leishmaniasis (Leishmania donovani) was eventually diagnosed; dengue NS1 remained detectable, an unusual persistence. Treatment with six doses of liposomal amphotericin B failed, followed by relapse. Serial testing showed dengue NS1, IgM, IgG becoming negative, revealing that dengue infection had resolved; active visceral leishmaniasis persisted and was then successfully treated with miltefosine. This case, reported in BMC Infectious Diseases, highlights how coinfection and altered immune response can obscure diagnosis: dengue and visceral leishmaniasis may influence each other’s test kinetics and clinical presentation, with imported VL cases into South Asia at risk for misdiagnosis.

Those with a history of chickenpox or herpes zoster generally do not need re-vaccination. If rash appears, seek medical care and report exposure history.

article.articleHeadline: A woman takes a bath, "washing out" a pulmonary infection; an old showerhead becomes a breeding ground for bacteria.
article.articleSummary: A case of Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) pulmonary disease linked to an old showerhead. A woman experienced recurrent cough, yellow-white sputum, and in severe episodes hemoptysis over three years, with multiple hospital visits and relief followed by relapse. MAC infections can resemble tuberculosis and be difficult to diagnose radiographically. Transmission may occur via inhalation; skin or mucous injuries may also allow entry, and even ingestion is possible. Preventive measures include regular descaling and replacement of showerheads; soak heads in 1:1 white vinegar and water for about 3 hours, scrub with toothbrush; limit shower time (5–10 minutes) and avoid long baths; gentle skin care. If persistent unexplained dry cough occurs, seek medical evaluation.

article.articleHeadline: Buruli Ulcer: The Silent Flesheater Hiding in Our Waters
article.articleSummary: Buruli ulcer, caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans in rural Ghanaian river basins, is a neglected tropical skin infection. It begins as a painless skin nodule near slow-moving rivers, swamps or wetlands; the toxin mycolactone damages tissue and suppresses local immunity, so initial lesions are painless with no fever. If untreated, progression leads to a large ulcer with deep tissue damage, potential scarring and disability. Transmission is not fully understood; environmental reservoirs exist with exposure through farming, fishing, or wading; minor skin breaks in muddy water may introduce bacteria. Children under 15 are disproportionately affected. Early treatment is highly effective with antibiotics (rifampicin plus clarithromycin or streptomycin) for several weeks, along with wound care and physiotherapy. Delays and reliance on traditional remedies worsen outcomes. Public health messages should promote prompt clinic visits for persistent painless skin lesions to prevent disability.

article.articleHeadline: Yellow fever confirmed in Sissala East after 21 mysterious deaths
article.articleSummary: Yellow fever has been confirmed in Sissala East Municipal, Ghana, after about 21 Fulbe deaths were investigated. Of four blood samples sent to Accra, one tested positive for yellow fever, establishing it as the probable cause, with six additional samples submitted to determine whether others are linked to yellow fever or another illness. Suspected cases have also appeared in Sissala West and Wa West, suggesting possible wider transmission beyond Sissala East. Yellow fever is transmitted by infected mosquito bites, not directly between people. Health authorities have launched a reactive response, including clinician sensitisation to identify and manage suspected cases; vaccination decisions will be made by national authorities in Accra, potentially targeting the affected area or specific groups. Residents are advised to sleep under insecticide-treated nets and reduce mosquito bites while authorities assess next steps.

article.articleHeadline: Mpox and domestic animals: the risk is not where many think.
article.articleSummary: Monkeypox (MPXV) remains a zoonosis. In 2022 outbreak, human transmission via close contact, including sexual contact, lesions, fluids, and contaminated materials, predominated. Dogs and cats are not natural reservoirs, and living with them is not a typical transmission route. The natural host is not definitively identified; evidence points to small mammals such as Funisciurus squirrels, ghiri, and giant rats. A 2026 Ivory Coast study in Nature documented a spillover from a Funisciurus squirrel to mangabeys, illustrating animal-to-human spillover as plausible. The 2003 US outbreak linked 47 human cases to prairie dogs infected after contact with imported mammals from Ghana. A 2024 CDC One Health study detected viral DNA on four dogs and one cat but found no viable virus or antibody response, suggesting environmental contamination rather than infection. Italian Ministry of Health and ECDC advise against fearing pets, urging avoidance of contact with animals if mpox is suspected or confirmed.

article.articleHeadline: How Ghana's Hotels and Restaurants Fought Back Against COVID-19: New
article.articleSummary: COVID-19 devastated Ghana’s hospitality sector, with Accra’s Metropolitan Area firms hit hardest as mobility restrictions (Executive Instrument E.I. 63) and the loss of international visitors collapsed demand. In a study of 90 senior managers from hotels, restaurants, shopping malls, car rentals and allied venues in the Greater Accra Region, researchers document a rapid cascade: revenue downturn, retrenchments, and fractured supply chains, compounded by the cancellation of international conferences. The work, conducted in 2020 and published in SN Social Sciences, confirms a pattern seen in other countries but emphasizes vulnerability in emerging economies with limited government support. Using a quantitative cross-sectional design and PLS-SEM with Confirmatory Factor Analysis, the study reports high measurement reliability (Cronbach’s alpha 0.979–0.987; composite reliability 0.981–0.990; AVE 0.795–0.898; loadings >0.70). Top resilience levers included prophylactic health programmes, equitable health infrastructure, and insurance uptake, enabling some firms to maintain operations and reassure customers.

article.articleHeadline: Marburg Virus Emerges Again: Ethiopia's First Outbreak Signals a
article.articleSummary: Marburg virus disease marked Ethiopia’s first outbreak, with suspected viral hemorrhagic fever in Jinka 12 November 2025; confirmed 14 November, outbreak declared over 26 January 2026. Four districts affected: Jinka, Malle, Arba Minch and Hawassa. Laboratory-confirmed 14 cases, 9 deaths (including two healthcare workers); five probable cases, all fatal. Case-fatality rate 64.3%. A review by Sherief Musa in the Journal of Emergency and Disaster Medicine synthesizes 70 studies (1968–2025) and WHO/CDC guidance, noting outbreaks are more frequent and dispersed, with Guinea (2021), Ghana (2022), Equatorial Guinea and Tanzania (2023), Rwanda (2024), and Ethiopia (2025) as recent examples. Marburg virus is Orthomarburgvirus marburgense, a non-segmented negative-sense RNA virus (Filoviridae), with two variants (Lake Victoria, Ravn). Genome ~19 kb, seven genes (NP, VP35, VP40, GP, L). Pathogenesis involves infection of mononuclear phagocytes, interferon suppression, cytokine storm, endothelial injury, DIC, liver and adrenal involvement, and hypovolemic shock.

article.articleHeadline: COVID-19 epidemic sweeps across Thailand — ABN 24.
article.articleSummary: COVID-19 infections in Thailand have not yet become an epidemic as of 20 September 2026, though the tourism sector is seeing reduced interest. Over the past four weeks, Thailand registered an average of about 15,000 new COVID-19 cases per week, still lower than the same period three years ago. Andrey Demin, head of the Russian Public Health Association, told Sputnik that the current trend should not trigger an epidemic, but cautioned especially for people over 60 and those with chronic diseases, since infection can be more severe in these groups. The Russian Association of Tour Operators said there are no grounds for concern and no signs of a mass outbreak that would significantly disrupt Russian vacations in Thailand. Thai authorities had previously reduced the visa-free stay for Russians from 60 days.

article.articleHeadline: In Thailand, they spoke about the danger of a tick-borne virus.
article.articleSummary: Thailand's Ministry of Public Health warned about the danger of tick-borne Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS). Montien Kanasavat, head of the Department of Disease Control, reported 10 SFTS infections in Thailand since 2012019, with 5 deaths. As of 16 September 2026, three cases have been recorded this year, with two fatalities. The illness disproportionately affects people over 50, often after exposure to ticks or domestic animals. Kanasavat urged vigilance, noting that some patients can rapidly progress to life-threatening disease. Early symptoms include high fever, headache, fatigue, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, and initial signs may resemble common infections, delaying recognition and response.

article.articleHeadline: Dr. Manoon warns of a surge in syphilis among youths; Stage 2 may have rashes all over the body even without fever or enlarged lymph nodes - Siam Rath
article.articleSummary: On 21 September 2026, Thai physician Dr. Manoon Leechawong warned of a surge in syphilis among youths in Thailand. A case from Vichaiyuth Hospital involves a 48-year-old Thai man with HIV on ART for 11 years and good viral control who developed a one-week diffuse erythematous rash on the trunk, arms, and thighs with itching, but no fever or oral ulcers, after unprotected sex two months earlier. Exam showed no fever, palms/soles spared, and no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests showed RPR reactive at 1:32 (previously negative 10 years ago and 7 years ago) and a positive Treponemal antibody, confirming syphilis. Diagnosed as secondary syphilis (syphilis stage 2) with HIV infection. The report highlights that secondary syphilis can present with widespread rashes without fever or enlarged lymph nodes, underscoring the need for testing and awareness amid rising outbreaks.
